description: Bloody Sunday, internment, IRA bombing campaigns, and how the Troubles reshaped British politics.
content_html:
The Origins of the Troubles

Northern Ireland had been created in 1921 as part of the partition of Ireland, when the predominantly Protestant and unionist counties of the north-east remained within the United Kingdom while the rest of Ireland became the Irish Free State. By 1968, Northern Ireland had a Catholic and nationalist minority — approximately one-third of the population — who faced systematic discrimination in housing, employment, and political representation under the Stormont government (Northern Ireland’s devolved parliament, dominated by the Ulster Unionist Party).

In 1968, inspired by the American civil rights movement and student protests in France, a civil rights movement emerged in Northern Ireland, demanding equal rights. The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) organised marches. A march in Londonderry/Derry on 5 October 1968, attacked by the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) with batons, was filmed and broadcast on television, shocking audiences in Britain and internationally. The Troubles had begun.

Key Fact

Catholic grievances in Northern Ireland included: discrimination in council housing allocation (properties systematically given to Protestant families); gerrymandered electoral boundaries that minimised Catholic representation; discrimination in public and private employment; and a special powers act that allowed detention without trial. These were not imaginary — independent investigations, including a 1969 Cameron Commission report, confirmed systematic discrimination.

The British Army and Escalating Violence

In August 1969, communal violence erupted on a large scale. Catholic areas of Belfast and Derry were attacked; houses burned. The RUC was unable to contain the violence. The Stormont government requested British Army assistance. British troops deployed to Northern Ireland on 14 August 1969 — initially welcomed by many Catholics as protection from Loyalist attacks. Within months, the relationship between the Catholic community and the army had deteriorated sharply.

The Provisional IRA split from the official IRA in December 1969. The Provisionals believed that the British state could only be removed by armed force. They began their bombing and shooting campaign in 1970. Violence escalated through 1970 and 1971. The British government, under Heath, faced mounting pressure to “do something.”

In August 1971, Heath’s government introduced internment — detention without trial. Operation Demetrius arrested 342 people on 9 August 1971. Almost all were Catholic or nationalist; Loyalist paramilitaries were largely untouched in the initial sweeps. The intelligence used was outdated and many arrested had no paramilitary connections. Fourteen of those detained were subjected to “five techniques” of interrogation involving hooding, noise bombardment, wall-standing, and sleep deprivation — later found by the European Court of Human Rights to constitute inhuman and degrading treatment.

Internment was a catastrophic political mistake. Rather than suppressing the IRA, it fuelled nationalist anger, swelled IRA recruitment, and alienated moderate Catholic opinion that had supported the civil rights path. Violence increased significantly after August 1971. The death toll for 1971 was 171; for 1972, the worst year of the Troubles, it rose to approximately 470 deaths.

Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972

On 30 January 1972, British paratroopers of the 1st Battalion Parachute Regiment shot dead fourteen unarmed civilians during a civil rights march in the Bogside area of Londonderry/Derry. A fifteenth person later died of wounds. The victims were all Catholic and nationalist. The soldiers opened fire claiming they had been fired at; witnesses and survivors denied this. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.

The immediate official inquiry (the Widgery Tribunal, 1972) largely exonerated the soldiers. Nationalists condemned it as a whitewash. The Irish government withdrew its ambassador from London. Thousands marched in Dublin; the British Embassy was burned. In Belfast and Derry, IRA recruitment accelerated massively. Bloody Sunday became the single most powerful symbol of British injustice in Ireland — a grievance that sustained Republican support for a generation. A second inquiry (the Saville Inquiry) was ordered in 1998 and its report, published in 2010, found that the shootings were “unjustified and unjustifiable” and that soldiers had fired on unarmed civilians. Prime Minister David Cameron issued a full apology in the House of Commons on the day of publication.

Key Fact

Bloody Sunday: 30 January 1972. Fourteen people shot dead (fifteen died including a later casualty) by British paratroopers in Londonderry/Derry. The Widgery Tribunal (1972) largely exonerated soldiers. The Saville Inquiry (1998–2010) found the shootings unjustified; PM Cameron apologised in 2010.

The IRA Bombing Campaign on the Mainland

The Provisional IRA extended its campaign to mainland Britain. In March 1973, car bombs exploded in central London, injuring over 200 people. The Guildford pub bombings of October 1974 killed five people. The Birmingham pub bombings of 21 November 1974 killed 21 people and injured 182 in the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs. It was the deadliest mainland attack of the campaign. Six men were convicted and imprisoned, but the “Birmingham Six” were subsequently found to have been wrongly convicted; their convictions were quashed in 1991.

The mainland campaign caused widespread public fear and political pressure on governments to find a solution. The Prevention of Terrorism Act was rushed through Parliament within two days of the Birmingham bombings, introducing powers to detain suspected terrorists for up to seven days and ban from mainland Britain individuals connected with Irish terrorism. The miscarriages of justice in the Birmingham Six and Guildford Four cases became a major issue of civil liberties in the 1980s and 1990s.

In March 1972, following Bloody Sunday, Heath’s government prorogued (suspended) the Stormont Parliament and introduced direct rule from Westminster. The Sunningdale Agreement of December 1973 attempted to create a power-sharing executive between Unionists and Nationalists, with an “Irish dimension” involving the Republic of Ireland. Unionists opposed the Irish dimension; the Ulster Workers’ Council called a general strike in May 1974. The strike brought Northern Ireland to a standstill and the power-sharing executive collapsed after fifteen days. Heath’s one attempt at a political settlement had failed.

Throughout the late 1970s, violence continued at a reduced but still deadly rate. In 1979, the IRA assassinated Lord Mountbatten (Queen Elizabeth’s cousin and a former Viceroy of India) off the coast of County Sligo, Ireland, and killed eighteen British soldiers at Warrenpoint, County Down, on the same day. The Troubles would not be resolved until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 — but in this period they profoundly reshaped British security policy and politics.
exam_tip_html: Northern Ireland questions require careful handling of contested history. Sources about Bloody Sunday will be sharply divided — British official sources (Widgery, 1972) vs nationalist accounts vs later official findings (Saville, 2010). For ‘5 marks — Source Utility’, always assess content AND provenance AND contextual knowledge together. A source from 1972 reflecting the immediate British government position is useful for understanding that position at the time, but limited as an account of what actually happened. For ‘10 marks — Compare Interpretations’, focus on WHY the interpretations differ: different standpoints (unionist vs nationalist, government vs civil rights movement), different evidence available (Widgery had limited access; Saville had thirty years of additional evidence), and different eras of writing.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Troubles began in 1968 with civil rights marches demanding equality for Catholics; escalated from 1969 with British Army deployment, the formation of the Provisional IRA, and internment (August 1971), which proved counterproductive.
  • Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) — 14 unarmed civilians shot dead by British paratroopers in Derry — was the most damaging single event for British credibility; not until 2010 did an official inquiry find the shootings unjustified.
  • The IRA mainland bombing campaign, including the Birmingham pub bombings (1974, 21 dead), caused widespread fear and miscarriages of justice; the Troubles reshaped British security policy and remained unresolved throughout this period.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the policy of internment introduced in August 1971.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- Internment allowed detention without trial; Operation Demetrius on 9 August 1971 arrested 342 people, almost all Catholic or nationalist.
- The policy backfired: it fuelled nationalist anger and IRA recruitment rather than suppressing the IRA; the 1972 death toll (approximately 470) was the worst of the Troubles.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the events of Bloody Sunday on 30 January 1972.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple cause identified, limited explanation.
Secure: Clear cause with explanation and factual support.
Mastering: Detailed explanation, precise evidence, chain of causation clear.

Causes may include:
- Continuing civil rights marches against internment brought thousands onto the streets of Derry despite a ban on marches; the army's presence at such events was already tense after months of violence.
- Escalating IRA violence and internment had created a confrontational atmosphere; paratroopers deployed believing intelligence that IRA snipers would be present.
- The previous deployment of the 1st Parachute Regiment in violent crowd control situations had conditioned soldiers to act aggressively; command and control failures on the day allowed an uncontrolled shooting incident.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Birmingham pub bombings of November 1974.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple consequence, limited development.
Secure: Clear consequence with explanation and evidence.
Mastering: Detailed consequence, precise evidence, wider significance addressed.

Consequences may include:
- The Prevention of Terrorism Act was passed within two days, introducing extended detention powers and travel bans — rushed legislation that critics later argued led to miscarriages of justice.
- Six men (the 'Birmingham Six') were wrongly convicted; their imprisonment until 1991 became a major civil liberties scandal and undermined confidence in the criminal justice system.
- Public hostility towards the Irish community in Britain intensified, with harassment and physical attacks on ordinary Irish people who had no connection to the IRA.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant were the events of Bloody Sunday in shaping the Troubles in Northern Ireland? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple points, limited evidence.
Developing: Some significance explained, basic evidence.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time addressed, evidence well-chosen.
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis, precise evidence, sustained argument.

At the time: fuelled massive IRA recruitment; the Irish government withdrew its ambassador; the British Embassy in Dublin was burned; Stormont was suspended and direct rule imposed in March 1972.
Over time: became the defining symbol of British injustice in nationalist memory; sustained Republican support for decades; the Saville Inquiry (1998-2010) and Cameron's apology (2010) showed it remained a live political wound for nearly four decades.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Internment was the most significant cause of the escalation of violence in Northern Ireland in 1971-1972.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement, little evidence.
Developing: Some evaluation, limited range of evidence.
Secure: Clear evaluation, agreement and disagreement addressed, factual knowledge used.
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation, precise evidence, substantiated overall judgement.

Agreement: internment swelled IRA recruitment; the 1972 death toll (approx. 470) was the worst of the Troubles; targeting almost exclusively Catholics alienated moderate nationalist opinion.

Disagreement: Provisional IRA violence had already escalated before internment; systemic discrimination and the events of 1969-70 had already created the conditions for violence; Bloody Sunday (January 1972) may have been as or more significant in sustaining the conflict; the removal of Stormont and imposition of direct rule contributed further.

[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the IRA mainland bombing campaign in the 1970s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail).

Features may include:
- The Birmingham pub bombings (21 November 1974) killed 21 people and injured 182 in the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs — the deadliest mainland IRA attack of the Troubles.
- The Guildford pub bombings (October 1974) killed five people; the Guildford Four were wrongly convicted — one of the major miscarriages of justice arising from the mainland campaign.

[4 marks total — 2 per feature]

glossary_terms.definition: A movement that emerged in Northern Ireland in 1968, campaigning for equal rights for Catholics and nationalists in areas including housing, employment, and voting, modelled partly on the American civil rights movement.

The period of communal conflict in Northern Ireland from the late 1960s to 1998, characterised by violence between Republican paramilitaries, Loyalist paramilitaries, and British security forces, with over 3,500 people killed.
The Provisional IRA (Irish Republican Army), a paramilitary organisation that split from the official IRA in December 1969 and waged an armed campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
Detention without trial, used in Northern Ireland from August 1971, when hundreds of people were arrested and held without charge.
30 January 1972, when British paratroopers shot dead fourteen unarmed civilians during a civil rights march in Londonderry/Derry — the bloodiest day of the Troubles in Northern Ireland.
IRA bomb attacks on two Birmingham pubs on 21 November 1974, killing 21 people and injuring 182 — the deadliest mainland IRA attack of the Troubles.
